newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK red chip prices to become volatile - Schroders.
newsitem.headline: HK red chip prices to become volatile - Schroders.

text.p: The share prices of China-backed and China-related companies listed in Hong Kong are likely to become increasingly volatile, Schroder Investment Management (Hong Kong) Ltd director David Lui said on Tuesday.

Red chips, or locally-listed stocks of Hong Kong companies with Chinese financial backing, recently saw a rally which pushed many to trade at more than 35 times 1997 earnings, compared with the average Hong Kong blue chip ratio of 15.
Lui told a news conference the gains were due mostly to expectation of future asset injections from parents, often municipal or provincial governments in China.

But red chips were the the most speculative sector of the Hong Kong market and investors must expect greater fluctuations in their prices as Beijing authorities produce fresh guidelines on asset injections, he said.
The market widely expects China to announce new guidelines on asset injections.
Lui also warned that margin lending by stockbrokers in Hong Kong to finance stock purchases, as well as lending by banks to stockbrokers, had risen sharply of late.
There was therefore an inevitable danger of investors becoming over-exposed if the prices of China-related stocks were to fluctuate, Lui said.

"In the longer term, sustaining the prices of red chips and China-related issues will depend not just on asset injections but also on the companies' ability to deliver earnings growth to justify their price/earnings ratings," he said.
"This is a function of the growth of China's economy, of the outlook for the sector, the regulatory environment and the quality of individual managements," he said.
A Schroder report released on Tuesday also said it expected H-shares, or shares of China-incorporated enterprises listed in Hong Kong, to continue to post "convincing" gains this year.

The sector had gained recently as investors began to look at quality Chinese firms with attractive valuations, until China's announcement last Thursday of a ban on state bank funds flowing into shares affected sentiment over H-shares, analsyts said.
"Despite the (recent) strong performance, we believed the China-related markets will continue to register convincing gains this year." the report said.
It was optimistic for another round of interest rate cuts in China around the end of June, it said.
The report noted the country's industrial production showed signs of recovery in the first quarter.
"We believe with stronger infrastructure investment and consumer spending in the second half of the year, the overall economy and corporate profits will begin to improve," it said.
H-shares generally posted disappointing results for 1996.
